analysis.one_liner: Applies federal wage, discrimination, and safety laws to Congress's own workplaces and employees.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 427-4 with both parties on board, and a Senate committee approved it, but no senator ever voted on it before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Members of Congress write wage, anti-discrimination, and workplace safety laws for everyone else, but their own offices have been exempt. This bill would have put Congress under the same laws it imposes on the rest of the country, including rules on pay, family and medical leave, discrimination, and job safety. It would have created an office inside the legislative branch to handle complaints, with counseling, mediation, a hearing, and court review as the route to a remedy. It passed the House almost unanimously, cleared a Senate committee, and then sat on the Senate's calendar until the Congress ran out without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 30,000 people who work for the House, the Senate, and congressional agencies — staffers, Capitol employees, and workers at offices like the Architect of the Capitol — would gain the same rights as other American workers: overtime and minimum-wage rules, protection from being fired or passed over because of race, sex, age, disability, or religion, unpaid family and medical leave, and a safe workplace. A new Office of Congressional Fair Employment Practices would give them an official channel for complaints instead of leaving disputes to the goodwill of their employer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Congressional employees, from staffers to Capitol workers

how_it_helps.text: The bill applies a list of core federal employment laws to the legislative branch: the Fair Labor Standards Act (wages and overtime), Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Family and Medical Leave Act, the Occupational Safety and Health Act, federal labor-management relations law, the Employee Polygraph Protection Act, the WARN plant-closing notice law, and the Rehabilitation Act [S2] [S5].

It would bar intimidation or retaliation against a congressional employee for using these rights, treating it as an unlawful employment practice remedied the same way as a violation of the underlying law [S2].

It establishes an Office of Congressional Fair Employment Practices inside the legislative branch, with a dispute process running from counseling and mediation to a formal complaint, a hearing, and review by a court or appeals board — so an employee would finally have a venue independent of the member or office they work for [S4] [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and congressional employing offices. They would bear the compliance costs of overtime and leave rules, face formal discrimination and safety complaints processed through the new office, and could have to pay awards from new settlement and awards accounts set up in House and Senate funds. The bill's drafters also softened the bite: members would not be personally liable for compensation, punitive damages are barred, and the process is confidential [S4] [S5].
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their offices

drawbacks.text: A congressional employee could not simply go to court. The bill makes its internal process the exclusive route: counseling, then mediation, then a complaint, and only then a hearing or court review — a slower and more restrictive path than an ordinary worker's [S4] [S5].

The counseling, mediation, hearings, and deliberations are confidential, with records made public only when required for judicial review — which would keep many disputes between members and their staff out of public view [S4] [S5].
The remedies are trimmed compared to ordinary law: punitive damages are barred, and no member of the House or Senate would be personally liable for paying compensation [S4] [S5].

It is explicitly not a violation to consider an employee's party affiliation, home state, or political compatibility in employment decisions for member, committee, and leadership staff — so political hiring and firing stays legal [S4] [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real and worthwhile: it ends the anomaly that the people who write workplace law are exempt from it, at the cost of building a new internal bureaucracy and trimming some remedies. An honest supporter would concede the confidentiality rules, the no-personal-liability rule, the ban on punitive damages, and the political-affiliation carve-out make the protections weaker than the versions Congress imposes on private employers, and the mandatory counseling-and-mediation steps add delay before an employee can reach a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 427-4, the Senate's Governmental Affairs Committee approved it and put it on the calendar, but Senate leaders never called it up for a vote before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, so the whole bill expired.

narrative.text: Representative Christopher Shays introduced the Congressional Accountability Act in the House on July 25, 1994, and 16 colleagues from both parties signed on as cosponsors — 7 Democrats, 8 Republicans, and 1 Independent [S6] [S7].
House committees reported the bill amended on August 2, the Rules Committee set floor procedures, and the House passed it on August 10, 1994, by 427 to 4 [S7] [S8].
The House vote was nearly unanimous across party lines: 251 of 256 Democrats and all 175 Republicans who voted were in favor, with only 4 Democrats opposed [S8].
The Senate received the bill on August 12, 1994, and referred it to the Committee on Governmental Affairs [S7].

On October 3, 1994, Senator John Glenn, the committee's chairman, reported the bill favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders — the list of bills waiting for floor time [S4] [S7].
No vote ever happened on the Senate floor. The bill stayed on the calendar until the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and every bill not passed by then dies and must start over [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and the offices that employ congressional staff came out ahead: they remained outside the wage, discrimination, leave, and safety laws the bill would have extended to them, and congressional employees kept whatever informal remedies existed inside their employing offices.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelming in both parties: 251 of 256 House Democrats and 175 of 178 House Republicans voted yes, and the 16 cosponsors split 7 Democrats, 8 Republicans, and 1 Independent.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and congressional employing offices
industries.note: The bill would have ended their exemption from wage, discrimination, family-leave, and safety laws and exposed them to formal complaints and awards paid through new settlement accounts. The drafters cushioned this: no personal liability, no punitive damages, confidential proceedings, and an explicit allowance for considering political affiliation in staff decisions [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Congressional employees (House, Senate, and agency staff)
industries.note: The roughly tens of thousands of people on congressional payrolls would gain the same legal rights as other American workers and an independent office to hear their complaints. Their gain is the direct cost to the members who employ them [S2] [S5].
